## 1. Grammar and morphology

The focal clause وَقَالُوٓا۟ أَسَـٰطِيرُ ٱلْأَوَّلِينَ ٱكْتَتَبَهَا is a nominal-sentence accusation embedded as the direct object of qālū. The predicate noun أَسَـٰطِيرُ (ʾasāṭīr, "tales") is tagged nominative; the accusative would be expected for a direct quotation object, so the nominative is best read as the opening of a quoted nominal sentence: "they said: '(These are) tales of the ancients…'". The genitive ٱلْأَوَّلِينَ is the muḍāf ilayh of the construct أَسَـٰطِيرُ ٱلْأَوَّلِينَ; the head ʾasāṭīr itself carries the case required by its syntactic role, here nominative as predicate of the quoted sentence.

The verb ٱكْتَتَبَهَا (iktatabahā) is Form VIII perfect, 3rd masculine singular, with a 3rd feminine singular suffix (the tales). Its subject is an unexpressed 3ms pronoun; the nearest antecedent in the discourse is the singular figure accused in 25:4 (ٱفْتَرَىٰهُ "he invented it", أَعَانَهُۥ "…helped him"), i.e. the messenger of 25:1, 25:7. The feminine pronoun هِىَ (hiya) resumes the tales as subject of the passive تُمْلَىٰ (tumlā, Form IV passive imperfect, 3fs): "so they are dictated/recounted ʿalayhi (to him)". The preposition عَلَىٰ with the 3ms suffix marks the recipient of the dictation — the same singular figure. بُكْرَةً and أَصِيلًا are indefinite accusative adverbials of time ("morning and evening").

Two grammatical observations are consequential:

(1) The syntactic frame of iktatabahā is transitive with a direct object (‑hā). Form VIII morphology alone does not settle whether the subject writes personally, writes for himself, or procures writing; that must be tested lexically and contextually (Stage 2). What the grammar does establish is that the writing event is predicated of the singular masculine subject, not of a plural scribe group — no plural agent appears in the clause.

(2) The passive tumlā ʿalayhi presents the same singular figure as recipient of dictation. The verse therefore predicates two distinct relations of one subject to the "tales": a perfect writing event (iktatabahā) and an ongoing passive reception (tumlā, imperfect). The fa- conjunction links them as consequence or elaboration within the accusers' claim.

## 2. Verse proximity analysis

The passage 25:4–5 forms a single accusation complex. In 25:4 the disbelievers make a compound charge: "this is nothing but a lie he invented (iftarāhu, Form VIII, 3ms) and other people have helped him in it (aʿānahu, Form IV)". Verse 25:5 then specifies the mechanism: the material is "tales of the ancients which he — the same singular subject — iktatabahā, and so they are dictated to him morning and evening."

The narrative logic is important. The accusers' principal allegation is that the revelation is fabricated (ʾifk, iftarāhu) with human assistance (qawmun ʾākharūn). Verse 25:5 elaborates the alleged source (ʾasāṭīr al-ʾawwalīn) and the alleged process (writing plus dictation). The Qurʾānic response in 25:6 does not engage the scribal mechanics; it answers on the level of origin and knowledge: "Say: He sent it down who knows the secret in the heavens and the earth." The rebuttal targets the fabrication charge, not the incidental description of how the accused handled text.

The surrounding verses reinforce the pattern. 25:7–8 continue the opponents' objections to the messenger's ordinary humanity (eating food, walking in markets), and 25:9 concludes that they have struck similitudes and strayed. The passage thus records a series of hostile claims whose truth the Qurʾān denies at the level of the principal allegation — that the revelation is humanly invented — while the phrasing of those claims incidentally presupposes a singular figure who writes and receives dictation.

Grammatically, nothing in 25:4–5 requires the writing to be delegated: the helper group of 25:4 is syntactically tied to ʾaʿānahu ("helped him"), while iktatabahā in 25:5 has the singular subject and direct object. Whether Form VIII lexically admits a procurement sense ("had written") is a lexical question deferred to pan-textual evidence; the immediate syntax predicates the writing of the singular subject, and the recipient of tumlā is that same subject.

## 3. Pan-textual evidence

**The iktataba question.** The verb ٱكْتَتَبَهَا (Form VIII of k-t-b) occurs exactly once in the Qurʾān, so no internal paradigm of this specific lemma exists. The Form VIII pattern must therefore be tested against other Form VIII verbs in comparable syntactic frames. The supplied corpus tags confirm Form VIII for ٱفْتَرَىٰهُ (25:4, iftarāhu), ٱفْتَرَىٰ (4:48), ٱتَّخَذُوا۟ (25:30, ittakhadhū), and لَّٱرْتَابَ (29:48, l-artāba). In each supplied case the subject performs the action directly: the fabricator fabricates, the takers take, the doubter doubts. None of these supplied instances denotes procuring another agent to perform the act. This is genuine, affirmative distributional evidence for the reflexive/self-directed character of Form VIII in the examined material. However, the examined set is a sample, not the full 963-verb inventory the indexed research claims to survey; the pattern is strongly supported by the verses actually supplied here, while exhaustive verification of all Form VIII occurrences remains outstanding.

**The 25:4 morphological contrast.** Within the same accusation complex, ٱفْتَرَىٰهُ (Form VIII, "he invented it") stands beside أَعَانَهُۥ (Form IV, "helped him"). The Qurʾān thus distinguishes, in one verse, an act predicated of the singular subject from assistance rendered by others. When the accusers wished to introduce other agents, they used a different construction (aʿānahu ʿalayhi qawmun ʾākharūn); iktatabahā in 25:5 carries no such auxiliary agent phrase. The syntactic parallel is probative: the same speakers, in consecutive verses, knew how to express delegated help and did not attach it to the writing verb.

**The ummī and 29:48 evidence.** 29:48 states the messenger did not recite any book before it nor write it with his right hand — a counterfactual whose force depends on the writing capacity being presupposed: "otherwise the falsifiers would have doubted." 62:2 describes the messenger as sent among al-ʾummiyyīn who يَتْلُوا۟ عَلَيْهِمْ ءَايَـٰتِهِۦ وَيُعَلِّمُهُمُ ٱلْكِتَـٰبَ — reciting and teaching the Book. 2:78 contrasts ʾummiyyūn who do not know the Book with those who do. These passages frame ummī as "without prior scripture" rather than "unable to write," and 29:48 in particular treats the absence of prior writing as the notable fact, not the absence of capacity.

**The dictation verb tumlā.** The root m-l-w in its supplied occurrences (3:178, 7:183) means God granting respite or extension — "we grant them increase." In 25:5 the Form IV passive tumlā ʿalayhi denotes material being read/recounted to the recipient. The supplied verses do not themselves fix whether the recipient then writes; that link comes from the accusers' own clause structure, which predicates iktatabahā of the same singular figure who receives the tumlā.

**The accusation's truth-status.** 6:25 and 8:31 record the identical charge ʾasāṭīr al-ʾawwalīn, and 25:6 answers it by appeal to the Sender's knowledge of the secret. The Qurʾān rejects the fabrication allegation; nothing in the rebuttal addresses the incidental mechanics of writing or dictation. 4:82 and 15:9 frame the epistemic alternative — divine origin guarded by God — without engaging scribal questions.

**Calibration.** (A) Explicit: Form VIII verbs in all supplied instances are self-directed; 25:4 contrasts Form VIII self-action with Form IV assistance; the singular subject of iktatabahā is the accused messenger. (B) Cumulative inference: the accusers' phrasing presupposes a figure who writes and receives dictation; the Qurʾān's rebuttal contests origin, not the described process. (C) Undetermined: whether Form VIII lexically excludes procurement in principle (external lexica record such senses; these are linguistic, not doctrinal, evidence); whether the full 963-verb survey claim is verified; whether the accusation's incidental description is historically accurate — an opponent's claim establishes what was alleged, not what occurred.

## 4. Qurʾān-centric research angles

- **Form VIII morphology and agency in Q 25:5** — Both indexed sources argue iktatabahā is reflexive ("he wrote them down himself"), since Form VIII's t-infix marks self-directed action and causative senses would require Form II (kattaba) or Form IV (aktaba); the 25:4 juxtaposition of iftarāhu (VIII) with aʿānahu (IV) is presented as the Qurʾān's own morphological control case (refs. 25:4, 25:5, 4:48, 25:30, 13:38, 2:8).

- **A corpus-wide survey of Form VIII verbs** — The sources claim a survey of 963 Form VIII verbs across 101 roots showing none denote delegated performance, with representative verbs (ittaqā, ittabaʿa, ittakhadha, iftarā, ihtadā, ikhtalafa, ibtaghā, ishtarā, iqtatala) uniformly self-directed or reciprocal; iktataba is the sole disputed occurrence (ref. 25:5).

- **Ummī as "without prior scripture," not illiterate** — The research reads al-nabiyy al-ʾummī (7:157) and 62:2 as describing a prophet raised among unscriptured peoples, with 29:48 and 3:75/3:20 supporting non-exposure to prior books rather than inability to write (refs. 3:20, 3:75, 7:157, 62:2, 29:48).

- **The Qurʾān as written revelation from the outset** — The sources argue the Qurʾān self-presents as kitāb from the beginning (2:2), with ṣuḥuf usage overwhelmingly textual (98:2, 80:13–15, 87:18–19, 53:36–37, 74:52), challenging the narrative of purely oral preservation followed by Uthmanic compilation (refs. 2:2, 98:2, 80:13, 80:15).

- **Theological influence on translation of Q 25:5** — The research contends that the doctrine of prophetic illiteracy led translators (e.g., Yusuf Ali's "caused to be written") to override the reflexive morphology, and that post-Qurʾānic lexicons expanded iktataba's sense under exegetical pressure (ref. 25:5).

history.content:
## 1. Grammar and morphology

Wa-qālū is perfect, third-person masculine plural, introducing direct speech. The quotation opens with the nominative noun phrase asāṭīru l-awwalīn, which stands as the quoted sentence’s topic without a copula. The focal verse contains no conditional, no prohibitive lā, and no ʾillā exception.

Iktatabahā is perfect, Form VIII, third-person masculine singular, active, with a feminine singular object suffix. The agent is encoded in the verb; the suffix -hā most plausibly resumes the non-human plural asāṭīr, since Arabic often uses feminine singular anaphora for non-human plurals. Form VIII’s t-infix can carry self-directed or self-benefactive nuance, but by itself it neither proves that he wrote in his own hand nor excludes “caused to be written.” The verb is active, not passive, so grammatically it predicates an action by the accused speaker with the tales as object; no additional agent is expressed in this clause.

Fa-hiya tumlā ʿalayhi consists of fa- plus a third-person feminine singular subject hiya and the passive imperfect Form IV verb tumlā, from m-l-w. The passive leaves the dictating agent unexpressed; ʿalayhi marks the recipient. The feminine singular subject agrees with the non-human antecedent. With ʿalayhi, the frame selects the dictation sense of mlw rather than its other sense of granting respite. Bukratan wa-aṣīlan are accusative temporal adverbials, specifying morning and later-day periods; they support ongoing or recurrent dictation, although the imperfect alone would not establish habituality.

The immediate dispute uses restriction constructions nearby: 25:4 has in hādhā ʾillā ʾifk, and 25:8 has in tattabiʿūna ʾillā rajulan masḥūran. These are negative restrictions, not conditional protases. In 25:7 lawlā introduces an optative challenge, also not a juridical conditional.

## 2. Immediate context

This verse is the second in a series of hostile objections. In 25:4 the disbelievers claim the recital is only a lie he fabricated and that another people helped him. In 25:5 they shift to a different allegation: the material is ancient legends, he has written them down, and it is dictated to him morning and evening. The sequence frames the claim as an accusation of human sourcing, not a factual description. 25:6 immediately answers that the one who knows the unseen sent it down.

Within 25:5, iktatabahā is active and attributes the writing to the accused messenger; tumlā is passive and leaves the alleged dictating source unnamed. This grammatical distinction matches the local rhetoric: the speakers assert his direct involvement in writing while leaving the suppliers of the material unspecified. The next verses continue the same disputational pattern. 25:7 objects that this messenger eats food and walks the markets and asks why no angel was sent down. 25:8 expands the challenge and ends with another restriction, claiming that the believers follow only a bewitched man. Thus 25:5 is a reported allegation in a longer sequence of rejection, not a Qurʾānic affirmation about how the recitation was produced.

## 3. Pan-textual evidence

The direct subject-matter passages cohere around two distinct points: the reported accusation and the Qurʾān’s written self-presentation.

**25:4–5** forms a single disputational block. In 25:4 the disbelievers say the recital is a lie he fabricated, *iftarāhu*, using a Form VIII verb with direct self-directed agency. Then 25:5 reports a second accusation: ancient tales, *iktatabahā*, followed by passive dictation to him. The grammatical shift is significant: the first clause predicates active writing by the accused subject; the second leaves the dictating agent unnamed. This matches the rhetoric of hostile allegation, not a Qurʾānic assertion of historical fact.

The same phrase *asāṭīr al-awwalīn* appears in **6:25** and **8:31** within rejection contexts. There the disbelievers dismiss the revelation as ancient legends, reinforcing that 25:5 is a reported accusation. **25:6** immediately answers with divine origin, not by denying the mechanics of writing.

**29:48** is central for the literacy claim. It states that before this revelation the messenger had not recited a prior scripture and had not written it with his right hand. The verse’s temporal limit is *min qablihi*, “before it.” It does not assert permanent illiteracy; it negates prior engagement with revealed scripture. This supports the article’s reading that the verse rules out dependence on earlier texts, not writing as such.

The *ummiyyūn* passages support the same semantic field. **2:78** defines *ummiyyūn* by their ignorance of the Book, not by inability to read or write: they know only wishes and follow assumption. **3:20**, **3:75**, and **62:2** contrast *ummiyyūn* with the People of the Book. **62:2** shows a messenger raised among the unscriptured people, teaching them the Book and wisdom. The cumulative contrast strongly favors “unscriptured” over “illiterate.”

The written nature of revelation is affirmed in **80:13–15**, **98:2**, **52:2–3**, and **3:3**. These describe honored pages, purified pages, inscribed book, and the Book sent down. **15:9** presents divine guarding of the Reminder. These verses establish that the Qurʾān presents itself as a written and preserved revelation; they do not by themselves make Muhammad the physical writer.

**Structural comparison:** The supplied Form VIII examples all show subject-directed or reciprocal action: *ittaqā*, *ittabaʿa*, *ittakhadha*, *iftarā*, *ihtadā*, *ikhtalafa*, *ibtaghā*, *ishtarā*, *iqtatala*. The direct contrast in 25:4 between *iftarāhu* and *aʿānahu* demonstrates the Qurʾān’s use of Form VIII for self-initiated action and Form IV for assisted or externalized agency. This supports the article’s morphological argument without making the full 963-verb survey verifiable from the supplied table.

## 4. Interpretation and CCC

**Coherence.** The focal clause *iktatabahā* is active, perfect, Form VIII, third-person masculine singular, with a feminine singular object suffix referring to the ancient tales. The subject performs the action. Nothing in the verse expresses a delegated agent for this verb. The passive *tumlā ʿalayhi* belongs to a separate predicate and gives no cause to convert the active writing into a causative procurement.

The immediate contrast with 25:4 is decisive. In one sentence the Qurʾān uses Form VIII for fabricated action and Form IV for external help. That pattern demonstrates that Form VIII is not the dedicated causative form. If the intended meaning were “he had them written,” the expected morphology would be Form II or IV, or Form X. The supplied examples across different roots reinforce this. Although the full Form VIII corpus claim was not exhaustively checked, every supplied example is consistent, and no supplied verse is a counterexample.

The article’s specific proposition is therefore supported: *iktatabahā* predicates direct action by the accused subject, not delegated scribal action. The verse remains a reported accusation; the Qur’ān in 25:6 rejects the accusation’s premise by asserting divine sending, not by denying that the wording says he wrote.

**Correspondence.** The restored manuscript evidence is external historical data. It may be examined for correspondence, but it carries no doctrinal authority. The cited early manuscripts and the uniformity of recitation correspond to the Qur’ānic claim of preservation in 15:9. However, they neither prove nor disprove the internal morphological conclusion about 25:5. Uncertainty in external compilation history does not downgrade the internal Qur’ānic finding.

**Calibration.**  
- **High confidence:** *Iktatabahā* is active and non-causative in this verse; Form VIII indicates direct subject action.  
- **High confidence:** *ummiyyūn* carries the sense of unscriptured or lacking prior revelation in the examined contexts.  
- **High confidence:** The Qur’ān presents revelation as written and guarded from inception in the supplied verses.  
- **Moderate inference:** The historical reconstruction that Muhammad personally wrote the revealed text throughout the whole revelatory period. This follows from the cumulative written-text verses and the removal of permanent illiteracy, but it is not an explicit single-verse declaration.  
No material internal counterevidence was identified against the precise claim.

## 5. Conclusion

The Qur’ānic conclusion is that 25:5’s *iktatabahā* predicates an active writing by the accused subject, not a delegated scribal action. The morphology, the immediate contrast in 25:4, and the wider Form VIII pattern support this. The causative interpretation lacks affirmative internal support. The verse is a reported accusation; its historical truth is not affirmed, and 25:6 responds with divine origin.

The broader Qur’ānic self-presentation as a written, preserved Book is strongly supported by 80:13–15, 98:2, 52:2–3, 3:3, and 15:9. The *ummiyyūn* passages further support the meaning “unscriptured” rather than “illiterate.” The only outstanding limitation is that the full survey of all Form VIII verbs was not individually verified; this is a coverage limit, not counterevidence. External manuscript data is consistent with preservation but does not control the internal finding. Confidence is high for the lexical-grammatical conclusion and the written-text self-presentation; moderate for the detailed historical reconstruction of who physically wrote each portion during the revelatory period.

The genitive ٱلْأَوَّلِينَ is the muḍāf ilayh of the construct أَسَـٰطِيرُ ٱلْأَوَّلِينَ; the head ʾasāṭīr itself carries the case required by its syntactic role, here nominative as predicate of the quoted sentence.

The verb ٱكْتَتَبَهَا (iktatabahā) is Form VIII perfect, 3rd masculine singular, with a 3rd feminine singular suffix (the tales). Its subject is an unexpressed 3ms pronoun; the nearest antecedent in the discourse is the singular figure accused in 25:4 (ٱفْتَرَىٰهُ "he invented it", أَعَانَهُۥ "…helped him"), i.e. the messenger of 25:1, 25:7. The feminine pronoun هِىَ (hiya) resumes the tales as subject of the passive تُمْلَىٰ (tumlā, Form IV passive imperfect, 3fs): "so they are dictated/recounted ʿalayhi (to him)". Two grammatical observations are consequential:

(1) The syntactic frame of iktatabahā is transitive with a direct object (‑hā). Form VIII morphology alone does not settle whether the subject writes personally, writes for himself, or procures writing; that must be tested lexically and contextually (Stage 2). What the grammar does establish is that the writing event is predicated of the singular masculine subject, not of a plural scribe group — no plural agent appears in the clause.

(2) The passive tumlā ʿalayhi presents the same singular figure as recipient of dictation. The verse therefore predicates two distinct relations of one subject to the "tales": a perfect writing event (iktatabahā) and an ongoing passive reception (tumlā, imperfect). The fa- conjunction links them as consequence or elaboration within the accusers' claim.

## 2. Verse proximity analysis

The passage 25:4–5 forms a single accusation complex. In 25:4 the disbelievers make a compound charge: "this is nothing but a lie he invented (iftarāhu, Form VIII, 3ms) and other people have helped him in it (aʿānahu, Form IV)". Verse 25:5 then specifies the mechanism: the material is "tales of the ancients which he — the same singular subject — iktatabahā, and so they are dictated to him morning and evening."

The narrative logic is important. The accusers' principal allegation is that the revelation is fabricated (ʾifk, iftarāhu) with human assistance (qawmun ʾākharūn). Verse 25:5 elaborates the alleged source (ʾasāṭīr al-ʾawwalīn) and the alleged process (writing plus dictation). The Qurʾānic response in 25:6 does not engage the scribal mechanics; it answers on the level of origin and knowledge: "Say: He sent it down who knows the secret in the heavens and the earth." The rebuttal targets the fabrication charge, not the incidental description of how the accused handled text.

The surrounding verses reinforce the pattern. 25:7–8 continue the opponents' objections to the messenger's ordinary humanity (eating food, walking in markets), and 25:9 concludes that they have struck similitudes and strayed. The passage thus records a series of hostile claims whose truth the Qurʾān denies at the level of the principal allegation — that the revelation is humanly invented — while the phrasing of those claims incidentally presupposes a singular figure who writes and receives dictation.

Grammatically, nothing in 25:4–5 requires the writing to be delegated: the helper group of 25:4 is syntactically tied to ʾaʿānahu ("helped him"), while iktatabahā in 25:5 has the singular subject and direct object. Whether Form VIII lexically admits a procurement sense ("had written") is a lexical question deferred to pan-textual evidence; the immediate syntax predicates the writing of the singular subject, and the recipient of tumlā is that same subject.

## 3. Pan-textual evidence

**The iktataba question.** The verb ٱكْتَتَبَهَا (Form VIII of k-t-b) occurs exactly once in the Qurʾān, so no internal paradigm of this specific lemma exists. The Form VIII pattern must therefore be tested against other Form VIII verbs in comparable syntactic frames. The supplied corpus tags confirm Form VIII for ٱفْتَرَىٰهُ (25:4, iftarāhu), ٱفْتَرَىٰ (4:48), ٱتَّخَذُوا۟ (25:30, ittakhadhū), and لَّٱرْتَابَ (29:48, l-artāba). In each supplied case the subject performs the action directly: the fabricator fabricates, the takers take, the doubter doubts. None of these supplied instances denotes procuring another agent to perform the act. This is genuine, affirmative distributional evidence for the reflexive/self-directed character of Form VIII in the examined material. However, the examined set is a sample, not the full 963-verb inventory the indexed research claims to survey; the pattern is strongly supported by the verses actually supplied here, while exhaustive verification of all Form VIII occurrences remains outstanding.

**The 25:4 morphological contrast.** Within the same accusation complex, ٱفْتَرَىٰهُ (Form VIII, "he invented it") stands beside أَعَانَهُۥ (Form IV, "helped him"). The Qurʾān thus distinguishes, in one verse, an act predicated of the singular subject from assistance rendered by others. When the accusers wished to introduce other agents, they used a different construction (aʿānahu ʿalayhi qawmun ʾākharūn); iktatabahā in 25:5 carries no such auxiliary agent phrase. The syntactic parallel is probative: the same speakers, in consecutive verses, knew how to express delegated help and did not attach it to the writing verb.

**The ummī and 29:48 evidence.** 29:48 states the messenger did not recite any book before it nor write it with his right hand — a counterfactual whose force depends on the writing capacity being presupposed: "otherwise the falsifiers would have doubted." 62:2 describes the messenger as sent among al-ʾummiyyīn who يَتْلُوا۟ عَلَيْهِمْ ءَايَـٰتِهِۦ وَيُعَلِّمُهُمُ ٱلْكِتَـٰبَ — reciting and teaching the Book. 2:78 contrasts ʾummiyyūn who do not know the Book with those who do. These passages frame ummī as "without prior scripture" rather than "unable to write," and 29:48 in particular treats the absence of prior writing as the notable fact, not the absence of capacity.

**The dictation verb tumlā.** The root m-l-w in its supplied occurrences (3:178, 7:183) means God granting respite or extension — "we grant them increase." In 25:5 the Form IV passive tumlā ʿalayhi denotes material being read/recounted to the recipient. The supplied verses do not themselves fix whether the recipient then writes; that link comes from the accusers' own clause structure, which predicates iktatabahā of the same singular figure who receives the tumlā.

**The accusation's truth-status.** 6:25 and 8:31 record the identical charge ʾasāṭīr al-ʾawwalīn, and 25:6 answers it by appeal to the Sender's knowledge of the secret. The Qurʾān rejects the fabrication allegation; nothing in the rebuttal addresses the incidental mechanics of writing or dictation. 4:82 and 15:9 frame the epistemic alternative — divine origin guarded by God — without engaging scribal questions.

**Calibration.** (A) Explicit: Form VIII verbs in all supplied instances are self-directed; 25:4 contrasts Form VIII self-action with Form IV assistance; the singular subject of iktatabahā is the accused messenger. (B) Cumulative inference: the accusers' phrasing presupposes a figure who writes and receives dictation; the Qurʾān's rebuttal contests origin, not the described process. (C) Undetermined: whether Form VIII lexically excludes procurement in principle (external lexica record such senses; these are linguistic, not doctrinal, evidence); whether the full 963-verb survey claim is verified; whether the accusation's incidental description is historically accurate — an opponent's claim establishes what was alleged, not what occurred.

## 4. Qurʾān-centric research angles

- **Form VIII morphology and agency in Q 25:5** — Both indexed sources argue iktatabahā is reflexive ("he wrote them down himself"), since Form VIII's t-infix marks self-directed action and causative senses would require Form II (kattaba) or Form IV (aktaba); the 25:4 juxtaposition of iftarāhu (VIII) with aʿānahu (IV) is presented as the Qurʾān's own morphological control case (refs. 25:4, 25:5, 4:48, 25:30, 13:38, 2:8).

- **A corpus-wide survey of Form VIII verbs** — The sources claim a survey of 963 Form VIII verbs across 101 roots showing none denote delegated performance, with representative verbs (ittaqā, ittabaʿa, ittakhadha, iftarā, ihtadā, ikhtalafa, ibtaghā, ishtarā, iqtatala) uniformly self-directed or reciprocal; iktataba is the sole disputed occurrence (ref. 25:5).

- **Ummī as "without prior scripture," not illiterate** — The research reads al-nabiyy al-ʾummī (7:157) and 62:2 as describing a prophet raised among unscriptured peoples, with 29:48 and 3:75/3:20 supporting non-exposure to prior books rather than inability to write (refs. 3:20, 3:75, 7:157, 62:2, 29:48).

- **The Qurʾān as written revelation from the outset** — The sources argue the Qurʾān self-presents as kitāb from the beginning (2:2), with ṣuḥuf usage overwhelmingly textual (98:2, 80:13–15, 87:18–19, 53:36–37, 74:52), challenging the narrative of purely oral preservation followed by Uthmanic compilation (refs. 2:2, 98:2, 80:13, 80:15).

- **Theological influence on translation of Q 25:5** — The research contends that the doctrine of prophetic illiteracy led translators (e.g., Yusuf Ali's "caused to be written") to override the reflexive morphology, and that post-Qurʾānic lexicons expanded iktataba's sense under exegetical pressure (ref. 25:5).
